question: Apple, Reliability Engineering IS&T Intern, first technical round (about 50 minutes, CoderPad). In the complexity and theory section the interviewer asked: **what does O(1) space complexity mean, and what is the difference between O(log n) and O(n) time? Give real-world examples.** The candidate explained the time-complexity difference using database indexing.
lookingFor: Correct understanding of Big-O as growth rate of resource use versus input size.
Knowing that space complexity counts extra memory, not the input.
Concrete real-world examples rather than memorised definitions.
Awareness of trade-offs such as time versus space.
answer:
**Big-O** describes how the running time or memory of an algorithm grows as the input size n grows, ignoring constants and lower-order terms. It is usually quoted for the worst case unless stated otherwise.

**O(1) space (constant auxiliary space).** The algorithm uses a fixed amount of *extra* memory regardless of n. It may read or modify an input of any size, but it only keeps a few variables (counters, pointers, a running sum). Examples: finding the maximum of an array with one variable, reversing an array in place using two indices, or checking for a palindrome with two pointers. Contrast with O(n) space: copying the array, building a hash set of all elements, or recursion that goes n levels deep (the call stack counts as space). Note that O(1) space does not mean O(1) time.

**O(log n) time.** Each step discards a constant fraction of the remaining work, usually half. Doubling n adds only one extra step. Examples: binary search on a sorted array, lookup in a balanced search tree, or a B-tree index in a database.

**O(n) time.** The work grows in direct proportion to n because every element is examined once. Examples: scanning a list for a value, summing an array, or a full table scan.

**Database indexing example.** Finding one row by id in a table of 1 million rows without an index means a full scan, up to about 1,000,000 row checks (O(n)). With a B-tree index, the database walks a few levels of the tree, around 3 or 4 page reads, which is O(log n). If the table grows 1000 times bigger, the scan gets 1000 times slower but the index lookup adds about one more level. The trade-off is extra storage and slower writes, because the index must be maintained.

Other everyday pictures: looking up a name in a printed phone book by repeated halving (O(log n)) versus reading it from page one (O(n)).
